Breast cancer stem cells as novel biomarkers Suman Kumar Ray a, Sukhes Mukherjee b,* a Independent Researcher, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh 462020, India b Department of Biochemistry, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh 462020, India ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Breast cancer Breast cancer stem cells Biomarker Precision medicine Therapeutics ABSTRACT Breast cancer is the most common cancer and the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Despite advancements in detection and treatment, it remains a major cause of cancer-related deaths in women. Breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs) are a crucial group of cells responsible for carcinogenesis, metastasis, medication resistance, and tumor recurrence. Identifying and understanding their molecular pathways is essential for developing effective breast cancer therapy. BCSCs are responsible for tumor genesis, development, metastasis, treatment resistance, and recurrence. Biomarkers are essential tools for identifying high-risk patients, improving diagnostic accuracy, developing follow-up programs, assessing treatment susceptibility, and predicting prognostic outcomes. Stem cell intervention therapy can provide specialized tools for precision therapy. Biomarker analysis in cancer patients is crucial to identify cells associated with disease progression and post-therapeutic relapse. However, negative posttherapeutic impacts can enhance cancer stemness by boosting BCSCs plasticity phenotypes, activating stemness pathways in non-BCSCs, and promoting senescence escape, leading to tumor relapse and metastasis. Despite the advancements in precision medicine, challenges persist in identifying stem cell markers, limiting the number of eligible patients for treatment. The diversity of biomedical research hinders the development of individualization-based preventative, monitoring, and treatment strategies, especially in oncology. Integrating and interpreting clinical and scientific data remains challenging. The development of stem cell-related indicators could significantly improve disease precision, enabling stem cell-targeted therapy and personalized treatment plans, although BCSCs are promising for breast cancer treatment optimization, serving as biomarkers for current therapy modalities. This summary discusses recent advancements in breast cancer stem cell research, including biomarkers, identification methods, molecular mechanisms, and tools for studying their biological origin and lineage development for precision medicine. 1. Introduction Breast cancer (BC) is a significant cause of cancer-related mortality for women globally, with metastasis being a major cause of death [1]. Breast cancer accounts for 12.5 % of all new annual cancer cases worldwide, making it the most common cancer in the world. BC is a heterogeneous disease with varying treatment responses and diseasespecific outcomes due to its wide range of subtypes and stages. Breast cancer, often linked to women, can also affect men, with male breast cancer accounting for about 1 % of all breast cancers, despite its lesser frequency compared to women. There are different types of female breast cancer including invasive ductal carcinoma, invasive lobular carcinoma, inflammatory breast cancer, Paget’s disease of the breast, angiosarcoma of the breast, phyllodes tumors, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS), HER2 status, triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) metastatic breast cancer etc. Gene expression profiling and immunohistochemistry (IHC) can be used to identify different subtypes of BC, such as TNBC, which

Breast cancer treatment varies across countries, with access to surgery and radiation therapy being crucial for improving outcomes. Recent advancements in targeting BCSCs have shown promise in increasing remission rates, but targeted therapy remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity. Tumor cells with a high potential for proliferation are first identified and eliminated, while cancer stem cells (CSCs) continue to live. A small percentage of tumor cells undergo therapy-induced senescence (TIS), which can alter the tumor microenvironment and have tumorpromoting effects. CSCs can result in tumor relapses and are resistant to treatment [6]. CSCs are present in breast cancer, with studies showing that xeno-transplanted cell subpopulations enriched for CSCs can produce tumors from a small fraction of unselected cells [7]. The CSC hypothesis suggests that cancer recurrence and metastasis are caused by this particular subpopulation of cells, as they are the only ones capable of forming tumors. Isolating candidate CSCs is essential to showcasing their functional traits, which has been made possible by the application of cell-surface markers and labeling of cells that display stemness-related traits. The discovery of CSCs in 1994 was made possible through various studies, including the identification of a small subset of cells proliferating slower than the mature blast cells [4]. These CSCs have distinct surface markers, which can be separated using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) or other immunoselection techniques [4]. Cancer is a complex and heterogeneous disease, with treatment failures and individual differences in effectiveness affecting overall survival rates. This highlights the need for personalized, targeted anticancer treatments to overcome these challenges. precision medicine involves measuring key tumor characteristics to determine the best therapeutic plan for each patient, effectively treating their cancer and preventing relapse [13,14]. The use of novel molecular analysis in cancer research has led to extensive data gathering. This article examines recent developments in precision medicine for BC, a frequent and fatal disease, focusing on the function of stem cells and BCSCs in this regard. This review also covers the present understanding of BCSC biomarkers, their relative abundance, and clinical significance in BC, techniques for BCSC identification and isolation, the mechanism controlling BCSCs and their potential for therapeutics, regarding the origins of BCSCs, and approaches for investigating BCSC lineage in precision oncology. This review article covers recent progress in breast cancer stem cell research, focusing on biomarkers, identification techniques, molecular mechanisms, and tools for understanding their biological genesis and lineage development in the context of precision medicine. 2. Origin of BCSCs The origin of tumors can be influenced by various factors, including the type of tumor, the type of stem cells, and the type of cell type [15]. Tissue-resident stem cells or their offspring may be the primary source of tumor start, which can occur during tissue regeneration, response to toxins, radiation, infections, or metabolic factors that result in mutations [5]. Tumor suppressors are inactivated, and oncogenes are overexpressed during the transformation process, allowing cells to proliferate out of control [16]. Tissue-resident stem cells have an infinite capacity for expansion, making them a potential source of tumors. Lineage tracing is a commonly employed method to monitor the movement, reproduction, and specialization of particular cells. Lineage tracing involves identifying all descendants of a single cell. Traditional single-cell lineage tracing assays have been the gold standard for determining the origin of a tumor. Still, this approach has limitations due to its reliance on a few markers [15]. The field of studying BCSC genesis has expanded with the advent of single-cell transcriptomics and single-cell genetic lineage tracing. The main theories about the development of BCSCs are the progenitor cells’ mutation-induced pluripotency into cancer stem cells (Fig. 1), the dedifferentiation of adult mammary cells into stem cells through the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and the generation of BCSCs from normal stem cells [4,17]. The hierarchical or CSC model assumes that only a tiny percentage of stem/progenitor cells within a tumor can replicate the tumor and reinforce the tumor hierarchy. In the linear hierarchy model of CSC creation, cancer is driven by transformation events in a stem or progenitor cell, leading to the development of more differentiated progeny as the tumor progresses. BCSCs have characteristics similar to minimally differentiated progenitor cells, including self-renewal, proliferation, and differentiation [4,18]. Research also indicates that differentiated mammary cells may become CSCs when exposed to harmful environmental factors like radiation and chemotherapy [19]. This hypothesis, known as clonal evolution or the stochastic model, postulates that all tumor cells have a comparable capacity to cause tumors and that intratumoral clonal evolution, caused by a series of mutations, results in tumor heterogeneity [20]. Cell stem cells in solid malignancies have a unidirectional hierarchy, meaning only the CSC population may prevent a tumor from growing. The clonal evolution model suggests that genetically unstable cells accumulate genomic and genetic alterations over time, leading to increased tumor aggressiveness, resistance, and heterogeneity [21]. The cellular plasticity model postulates that various cellular states can interconvert, explaining why these models are not mutually exclusive [22]. The lineage tracing test in mice models is currently the gold standard for defining the origin of BCSCs, enabling tracking of an animal singlecell clone by labeling different cell subpopulations with different cellspecific promotors [4]. The most popular method for monitoring the migration, division, and proliferation of certain cells in vivo is lineage tracing. From a molecular and cellular biology standpoint, lineage tracing has broadened the platforms accessible for drug screening, cell plasticity research, disease model building, and the development of customized medicine. Lineage tracing offers fresh perspectives on the growth and regeneration of digestive organs as well as methods for identifying the etiology and course of digestive diseases. However, recent developments in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) have enabled the objective characterization of molecular states and cell identities in heterogeneous tissues at an unprecedented resolution [23]. Methods for the identification and isolation of breast cancer stem cells Four primary methods are used for identifying and isolating BCSCs are based on their functional characteristics or high expression of cell surface markers [4]. A popular technique is based on specific cell surface indicators or combinations of biomarkers, which is a top focus in cancer research (Table 1). Other techniques, such as mammosphere formation, ALDEFLUOR assay, and side population cell isolation using Hoechst 33342, are based on intrinsic properties of CSCs, such as high expression of ALDH1, ATP-binding cassette transporters, and CSC self-renewal and proliferation [4]. 4. Therapy-induced senescence: its hallmarks, biomarkers, and its role in BCSC generation Senescence is a process in cancer cells that occurs when exposed to DNA damage agents like radiation and chemotherapy [30,31]. This process, known as tumor suppressor senescence (TIS), has been extensively studied due to its significant impact on patients’ long-term outcomes. TIS is initiated and maintained by activating one or more tumor suppressor pathways, such as p53, p16 (Ink4a), p21 (Waf1), and retinoblastoma (RB) [5]. Cancer cells deficient in functional p53 and RB protein can still cause the senescence phenotype. Senescence and TIS have negative effects on treatment outcomes and prognoses, but they also attract immune cells, cause inflammation, and eliminate senescent tumor cells [5]. However, senescence can enhance CSC development by playing a significant pro-tumorigenic role. Classical biomarkers of cellular senescence include senescence-associated beta-galactosidase (SA-ß-gal) activity, p53 protein expression, nuclear p53 concentration, p14 (Arf), p16 (Ink4a), and p21 (Waf1) upregulation, SASP, and frequently senescence-associated heterochromatic foci (SAHF) [5]. Senescent cells also exhibit levels of heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) gamma, histone H3 di- or tri-methylated lysine 9 (H3K9Me2/3), and histone H2A variant (macroH2A) [32]. To accurately evaluate the pathological fate of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC), it is necessary to verify the concurrent expression of several markers associated with the p53 pathway [33]. In cancers, innate and adaptive immune cells form a ‘senescence surveillance’ mechanism when induced, preventing premalignant cells from undergoing cancer growth [31,34]. More research is needed to demonstrate the significance of the chemokine axis in initiation and maintenance of senescence and ensure adequate immune surveillance. Signaling pathways such as Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog, and Hippo play a crucial role in regulating the self-renewal of BCSCs. The Notch signaling pathway is a crucial signaling cascade involved in the preservation of the BCSC phenotype [43]. It is essential for self-renewal, stem cell maintenance, and cellular differentiation during the developmental stage of cells. Notch signaling controls stem cell proliferation and differentiation into luminal progenitor cells in the mouse mammary gland. In the xenograft model, γ-secretase inhibition prevented the development of the active Notch intracellular domain (NCID), thereby stopping tumor growth [44] and decreasing the populations of CD44+/CD24� /low and ALDH + BCSCs. Overexpression of the Notch ligand DLL1 leads to increased Notch signaling, which in turn stimulates angiogenesis, migration, proliferation, and the CSC phenotype [45]. The abbrent Wnt/ β-catenin signaling system supports the renewal, proliferation, and differentiation of BCSC. Wnt/β-catenin signaling is one of the most important mechanisms controlling stem cell division and self-renewal [46,47]. Oncogenic stimulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling increases the development of human mammospheres and enriches mammary stem and progenitor cells. Wnt signaling contributes to BC chemoresistance and radioresistance, but blocking Wnt/β-catenin signaling inhibits the CSC-like phenotype, which reduces breast cancer metastasis [48]. The Canonical Wnt signaling pathway, which relies on β-Catenin and T cell factor (TCF)/lymphoid enhancer factor (LEF), primarily regulates breast cancer cell proliferation and the maintenance of ’stemness’. Notch signaling regulates the differentiation of breast epithelial cells in the course of normal development. Different studies have shown that the Notch system significantly contributes to the advancement of breast cancer by involving the overexpression and/or aberrant genetic expression of notch receptors and ligands, which regulate angiogenesis. Hypoxia-induced up-regulation of Notch ligands led to the activation of Notch signaling. HIF-2α facilitated the transformation of stem cell characteristics by stimulating Notch and Wnt pathways in breast cancer cells. HIF-2α overexpression can trigger both Wnt and Notch signaling, which in turn supports the stem cell phenotype, treatment resistance, and overexpression of BCSC markers [49]. The hedgehog (Hh) pathway is a major regulator of cell fate and plays a significant role in cellular activities during embryonic development [50]. Proliferation, migration, metastasis, and aggressiveness of BC have all been linked to overexpression of the major Hh pathway regulators, SHH, DHH, PTCH1, and GLI1. The Hh/GLI signalling pathway involves ligands (Shh, Ihh, and Dhh), transmembrane receptors (Ptch1 and Ptch2), transcription factors (GLI1-3), and signalling regulators that collaborate to either inhibit or stimulate (Shh, Ihh, Dhh, SMO, GLI1-3) the signalling process. There was significant variation in the expression of Hippo genes among different subtypes of breast cancer. DNA methylation may regulate the Hippo pathway in breast cancer cells. The Hippo pathway, crucial for organogenesis and regeneration [51], is another significant circuit involving CSCs. It consists of a core transcriptional module and a core regulatory kinase module. The Hippo pathway is crucial for maintaining tissue homeostasis by balancing proliferation and differentiation. The pathway functions via a series of kinases that ultimately activate the Yes-associated protein (YAP) and its paralog, the transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ). TAZ is a transcriptional regulator that is often activated in human cancers. Recent studies show that TAZ is crucial for the development or progression of the majority of solid tumours. Their activation triggers the characteristics of cancer stem cells, including proliferation, resistance to chemotherapy, and the spread of cancer to other parts of the body. TAZ expression is significantly higher in tumors generated from BCSCs than in tumors not derived from BCSCs [52]. The BCSC pool’s upkeep has been linked to the interaction between TAZ and the extracellular matrix. Treatment with Dasatinib, a multi-target kinase inhibitor, demonstrated the ability to destroy the CSC population selectively [53]. Dasatinib belongs to a category of drugs known as kinase inhibitors. It functions by inhibiting the activity of an aberrant protein that stimulates cancer cells to proliferate. This inhibits the proliferation of cancer cells. Dasatinib enhances the sensitivity of KRAS-mutant cancer cells to mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase inhibitor via inhibiting TAZ activity. 6. BCSC subpopulations and role of non-coding RNAs in BCSCs Research has identified nonoverlapping cell groups in primary human breast tumors using CD44+/CD24� /low and ALDH1 biomarkers [4]. BCSCs with the ALDH1 + phenotype exhibit an epithelial and proliferative phenotype, similar to luminal stem cells, while those with CD44+/CD24� /low markers exhibit a mesenchymal and quiescent phenotype similar to basal stem cells [4]. BCSCs can revert between mesenchymal and epithelial states during EMT, under cytokine signaling control. Both BCSC populations shared the ability to replicate a tumor in a xenograft model. However, neither ALDH1 + BCSCs nor CD44+/CD24� /low BCSCs exhibit 100 % sphere forming capability in vitro [4]. The most tumorigenic and metastatic activity is exhibited by tiny populations of BCSCs that simultaneously express both ALDH1 + and CD44+/CD24� /low biomarkers, capable of forming tumors [4,54]. Other miRNAs function as tumor suppressors, reducing BCSC stemness or reverse treatment resistance when overexpressed. These miRNAs regulate BCSC self-renewal, tumor metastasis, and treatment resistance through various pathways. Some miRNAs, such as Let-7, miR-146, miR-142, miR-374, miR-600, and miR340, regulate the Wnt signaling pathway and the BCSC phenotype [4]. Long intergenic non-coding RNAs (LincRNAs) can finely adjust the expression of nearby genes with unique tissue specificity through various means, showcasing our developing knowledge of the non-coding genome. LincRNAs, which are longer than 200 nucleotides and do not code for proteins, can interact with miRNAs to affect the stability of mRNAs or attract transcription factors to control gene expression [56]. Relative BCSCs abundance in different breast cancer subtypes and their clinical relevance Breast cancer subtypes have varying proportions of CD44+/CD24� / low BCSC subpopulations, with basal-like tumors having larger proportions than luminal type tumors [54]. The CD44+/CD24� /low phenotype is enriched in basal/mesenchymal BC cell lines, while the CD44� /low/CD24 + cell population is enriched in luminal cell lines. A current research indicates that individuals with TNBC and metastatic BC who exhibit the CD44+/CD24� /low phenotype have a poor prognosis [59]. However, inconsistent findings may be due to using various BC subtypes in separate studies or distinct patient cohorts. Studies have shown that varying expressions of CD44/CD24 and ALDH1 in distinct subtypes of breast cancer. The CD44+/CD24� /low phenotype is predominantly found in basal-like breast cancers, whereas ALDH1 + cells are more prevalent in HER2-overexpression (HER2-OE) and basal/epithelial breast cancers. A subgroup of BCSCs is identified by elevated expression of ALDH1, which is correlated with a poor prognosis for TNBC patients [60]. ALDH activity is thought to be a better prognostic marker for BCSCs. TNBCs display variable BCSC abundances and ratios of mesenchymal or epithelial BCSC subtypes. HER2+ BC is characterized by a high proportion of ALDH1+ epithelial BCSCs, but at a lesser proportion than TNBC [4,61]. HER2 is selectively expressed in HER2� /ER+ luminal BCSCs and tightly controls genes involved in stem cell and progenitor cell regulation. New targeted approaches and therapeutic drugs targeting BCSC subpopulations Two hypotheses explain how BCSCs become multidrug resistance (MDR) in BC that show elevated resistance to standard chemotherapy treatments [5]. The first hypothesis suggests that only BCSCs expressing ATP-binding cassette transporters (ABC transporters) can repopulate the tumor by asymmetrical cell division following exposure to anticancer drugs. The rising evidence that CSCs contribute to cancer development and recurrence suggests that developing anti-CSC medicines will likely enhance cancer patients’ long-term survival rates. A proof of principle for targeting CSCs was demonstrated in Acute myeloid leukemia (AML, a type of cancer that starts in the blood-forming cells of the bone marrow), where the anti-leukemia medication TDZD-8 selectively destroyed leukaemia stem cells while not impacting normal hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells [67]. Many of the mechanisms now being investigated as possible therapeutic targets in CSCs have been proven to govern normal stem and progenitor cells, thus identifying techniques to selectively target the pathways in cancer including breast cancer will be crucial. Recent research has focused on Notch and Wnt pathways as regulators of cell destiny in the breast [68-71]. It’s not surprising that they could be therapeutic targets in CSCs. In a model of Notch1-driven mammary carcinogenesis, inhibiting Notch signaling caused tumor regression and decreased tumorsphere development in vitro [72]. In response to hypoxia, the Notch ligand Jagged2 was upregulated in breast cancer cells and bone marrow derived cells, resulting in CSC growth [73]. Notch 4 activity is increased in breast CSCs, and Notch and Wnt signaling were found to mediate radio-resistance in breast progenitor and CSCs [74-76]. Pygo2, a Wnt co-activator, augmented mammosphere formation in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells [77]. In contrast, pygo2 deletion in MMTV-Wnt1 tumor cells reduced both mammosphere and tumor-forming capability [78]. The discovery of Salinomycin in a screen for CSC inhibitors highlighted the potential therapeutic value of targeting Wnt signaling. Salinomycin selectively eliminates CSCs by blocking Wnt signaling and triggering apoptosis [79-81]. Salinomycin also destroyed iCSCL-10A cells resistant to Taxol and Actinomycin D [82]. Metformin targets CSC and can work together with chemotherapeutic medications to lower CSC levels and tumor progression [83,84]. Metformin may be effective for treating TAM-resistant ER + malignancies that upregulate NF-κB [85]. Research has shown the diversity in responses of multiple human BC cells to different anticancer agents, with the expression levels of molecular markers of BCSCs being correlated with the chemotherapeutic effect of anticancer agents. The potential use of CSCs and their markers in the customization of treatment regimens in breast neoplasia suggests the potential of using CSCs and their markers in pre- and post-chemotherapy initiation [101,102]. CSCs play a crucial role in factors such as tumorigenicity, metastasis, chemo/radioresistance, and multidrug resistance in anticancer treatment. Research has focused on molecules associated with CSCs that function as markers of recognition and differentiation and targets for their selective treatment. CSC markers may be crucial for their identification or targeting, and they can serve as valuable tools for treatment tailoring [101]. The variability in the chemotherapeutic/ cytotoxic effect of anticancer agents in human BC cells is correlated with the expression levels of several molecular markers of BCSCs, suggesting that these markers may be used as biomarkers in the fight against BC. 10. Conclusions and future perspectives The study examines the expression of potential CSC markers in primary breast carcinomas, finding that all markers had a high correlation with negative ER status. Additional markers are needed for IHC quantification of CSCs in ER + tumors, which account for 75-80 % of all breast cancers. The most potent predictor of outcome in ER-disease was a composite score representing the expression of all four markers, although only ITGA6 maintained independent prognostic relevance.
